title: Nine giant building projects that were seriously backed — and why only one is rising
summary: Backed by Tokyo builders, Saudi Arabia's wealth fund and Hong Kong's government, the schemes range from a pyramid over the bay to a ribbon to space — most are blocked because the ultra-strong material can't be made at scale or the budgets dwarf their funders.

claims.text: Shimizu Mega-City Pyramid (TRY 2004) is a proposed 2,004m (2km, 6,575ft) tall pyramid over Tokyo Bay, about 14 times the height of the Great Pyramid of Giza and ~2.5x the Burj Khalifa.

sources.title: In 2004, Japanese engineers proposed a mile-high pyramid over Tokyo Bay

claims.text: The pyramid is designed to house 750,000 to 1,000,000 people and would be the largest man-made structure on Earth if built.

sources.title: In 2004, Japanese engineers proposed a mile-high pyramid over Tokyo Bay

claims.text: The pyramid's structural concept is an open lattice of megatrusses supporting 36 engineered concrete piers, with 24+ 30-storey skyscrapers suspended inside by cables and connected by moving walkways/tilted elevators/pods; trusses would be clad in solar film plus algae power and designed to flex in earthquakes/wind/tsunami.

sources.title: In 2004, Japanese engineers proposed a mile-high pyramid over Tokyo Bay

claims.text: Shimizu's pyramid cannot be built with conventional steel/concrete; it depends on future mass-produced carbon-nanotube and graphene materials whose real-world tensile strength (11-120 GPa in lab) remains far below theoretical ~200 GPa due to defects.

sources.title: In 2004, Japanese engineers proposed a mile-high pyramid over Tokyo Bay

claims.text: Shimizu has stated construction could begin as early as 2030 with completion around 2110 (80-year build); the project remains a paper thought-experiment with patents filed from 1992, inspired by Blade Runner (1982).

sources.title: In 2004, Japanese engineers proposed a mile-high pyramid over Tokyo Bay

claims.text: Shimizu Ocean Spiral is Shimizu Corporation's third Dream Series concept (announced Nov 2014) developed over 2 years with Tokyo University, Saga University and JAMSTEC.

sources.title: A vision of the future? We can't take our eyes off Shimizu Corporation's Ocean Spiral design

claims.text: Ocean Spiral consists of a 500m-diameter (1,640ft) floating sphere (Blue Garden) housing 5,000 people over 75 floors, stabilized by buoyancy-gravity balance and able to fully submerge in tsunami/typhoon, connected by a 15km spiral tube descending 3,000-4,000m to a seabed resource plant.

sources.title: A vision of the future? We can't take our eyes off Shimizu Corporation's Ocean Spiral design

claims.text: Ocean Spiral would also include deep-sea fish farms, seawater desalination, and seabed mineral mining via the Earth Factory; energy would be generated from the seabed.

sources.title: A vision of the future? We can't take our eyes off Shimizu Corporation's Ocean Spiral design

claims.text: Shimizu estimated Ocean Spiral would cost over 3 trillion yen (US$25.4bn), take 5 years to build, with technology ready between 2030-2050.

sources.title: A vision of the future? We can't take our eyes off Shimizu Corporation's Ocean Spiral design

claims.text: Obayashi Corporation announced in 2012 a space elevator to be built by 2050, comprising a 96,000km carbon-nanotube cable, a 400m-diameter floating Earth Port, and a 12,500-ton counterweight, with capacity for 100-ton climbers.

sources.title: The Space Elevator Construction Concept

claims.text: Obayashi's concept includes stations at Low Earth Orbit Gate, Geostationary Orbit (36,000km), Mars Gate and Solar System Exploration Gate; climbers would ascend at ~200 km/h carrying ~30 passengers, taking about a week to GEO.

sources.title: The Space Elevator Construction Concept
A Japanese company is about to test a tiny space elevator in space

claims.text: Obayashi's own simulation concludes construction is technically feasible only with assumed cable tensile strength of 150 GPa, requiring ~20 years to build the cable (initial 20-ton cable reinforced 510 times to 7,000 tons over ~18 years, plus 1 year for facilities), with small wind/Coriolis effects and need for ground pre-tension.

sources.title: The Space Elevator Construction Concept

claims.text: No material at required scale/strength exists today; carbon nanotubes have theoretical breaking length ~5,000-6,000km but real production cannot make defect-free continuous 96,000km ribbon; diamond nanofilament proposed but also not scalable.

sources.title: A Japanese company is about to test a tiny space elevator in space
The Space Elevator Construction Concept

claims.text: A first tether-climber test (STARS-Me, Shizuoka University + Obayashi) flew in 2018: two 10cm CubeSats with 10m tether and matchbox-sized motorized climber, the first climber movement on a tether in space.

sources.title: A Japanese company is about to test a tiny space elevator in space

claims.text: Saudi Arabia's The Line at NEOM is designed as a pair of parallel mirrored walls 170km long, 500m high, 200m wide, enclosing 34km2, planned for 9 million residents at density ~265,000/km2 (10x Manhattan).

sources.title: Staff at France's EDF question involvement in futuristic Saudi city
End of the Line? Saudi Arabia ‘forced to scale back’ plans for desert megacity

claims.text: The Line is part of NEOM (26,000km2 in Tabuk Province), centrepiece of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's Vision 2030 to diversify from oil, backed by the Public Investment Fund (PIF) with initial $500bn commitment; internal estimates rose to $1.6tn (2021) then ~$4.5tn (2022).

sources.title: End of the Line? Saudi Arabia ‘forced to scale back’ plans for desert megacity
How Saudi Arabia's futuristic megacity will progress in 2026

claims.text: Construction on The Line began July 2023 with large earthworks; by Oct 2024 NEOM reported a SAR 700m concrete factory (20,000 m3/day) and ~1,000 of 30,000+ foundation piles placed, with 120 piles/week; PIF reported 115,000 workers/contractors, 100+ sites, 20M m3 earth excavated in 2024.

sources.title: How Saudi Arabia's futuristic megacity will progress in 2026

claims.text: The Line has been scaled back: Bloomberg-reported documents indicate the 2030 target cut from 1.5 million people over 16km (20 modules) to ~300,000 people in a 2.4km (1.5-mile) segment; at least one contractor dismissed workers.

sources.title: End of the Line? Saudi Arabia ‘forced to scale back’ plans for desert megacity

claims.text: By late 2025 construction on The Line was effectively suspended: Hyundai E&C cancelled SAR 6.16bn (~$1.6bn) tunnel contract, workforce cut ~35% with 1,000+ employees relocated to Riyadh, CEO Nadhmi Al-Nasr departed Nov 2024, and 2029 Asian Winter Games reassigned from Trojena (Feb 2026).

sources.title: How Saudi Arabia's futuristic megacity will progress in 2026

claims.text: Oceanix Busan is billed as the world's first prototype floating city, developed by Oceanix (NY blue-tech, founded 2018) with UN-Habitat and Busan Metropolitan City, designed by BIG-Bjarke Ingels Group and SAMOO (Samsung) with Arup, Bouygues, MIT Center for Ocean Engineering.

sources.title: UN-Habitat and partners unveil Oceanix Busan - world's first prototype floating city

claims.text: Oceanix Busan initial phase is 6.3 hectares (15.5 acres) of three interconnected hexagonal platforms (living/research/lodging) for 12,000 residents, expandable to 20+ platforms for up to 100,000, linked to land by bridges, with net-zero energy (floating/rooftop PV), closed-loop water, waste, food, and habitat regeneration.

sources.title: UN-Habitat and partners unveil Oceanix Busan - world's first prototype floating city

claims.text: Oceanix Busan was unveiled at UN Headquarters April 2022; construction was slated to begin 2023 with completion 2025-2028 tied to Busan's Expo 2030 bid; UN-Habitat said in May 2024 it was being implemented off Busan's North Port, but no full city is yet operational and broader scaling remains uncertain due to cost/regulation.

sources.title: UN-Habitat and partners unveil Oceanix Busan - world's first prototype floating city

claims.text: Hong Kong's Lantau Tomorrow Vision (now Kau Yi Chau Artificial Islands) proposes 1,700 hectares of reclamation (1,000 ha at Kau Yi Chau plus Sunny Bay/Lung Kwu Tan) to create a third central business district with 190,000-210,000 flats for 550,000 people and 4M sqm office space.

sources.title: Hong Kong shelves controversial Lantau reclamation; ‘necessary conditions’ missing
Price tag for artificial islands off Hong Kong's Lantau balloons to HK$580 billion

claims.text: Lantau Tomorrow Vision was announced by Chief Executive Carrie Lam in Oct 2018 with initial estimate HK$624bn (US$80bn) including HK$273bn transport network (56km roads/rail); cost later revised to HK$580bn (US$74.6bn).

sources.title: Price tag for artificial islands off Hong Kong's Lantau balloons to HK$580 billion
Hong Kong shelves controversial Lantau reclamation; ‘necessary conditions’ missing

claims.text: Hong Kong government has shelved Lantau reclamation: Development Secretary Bernadette Linn stated Sept 2025 the government lacks 'necessary conditions' to start within the current term, halting environmental assessment and prioritizing the 30,000-hectare Northern Metropolis near the mainland border; first population intake originally 2032, reclamation start delayed from 2025 to 2027 then indefinite.

sources.title: Hong Kong shelves controversial Lantau reclamation; ‘necessary conditions’ missing

claims.text: Jeddah Tower (Kingdom Tower) in Jeddah Economic City is designed by Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture to exceed 1,000m (1,008m/3,281ft, 167 floors, 530,000 sqm), the first building over 1km, 170m taller than Burj Khalifa (828m, also by Smith at SOM).

sources.title: World's Tallest Skyscraper Hits Major New Construction Milestone

claims.text: Jeddah Tower is centrepiece of a $20bn, 57M sq ft Jeddah Economic City district, with 7 hotel floors, 11 luxury apartment floors, offices, and world's highest observation deck at 660m.

sources.title: World's Tallest Skyscraper Hits Major New Construction Milestone

claims.text: Jeddah Tower construction paused in 2018 for 7 years due to contractor/financing issues (Saudi Binladin Group, anti-corruption purge); Saudi Binladin Group rehired late 2024 on SR7.2bn ($2bn) contract, Turner Construction took project management March 2025, and construction restarted Jan 2025 advancing ~1 floor per 3-4 days.

sources.title: World's Tallest Skyscraper Hits Major New Construction Milestone

claims.text: As of late 2025 Jeddah Tower had reached 69-80 floors / 454m at 113 floors (reports vary by date), targeting 500m halfway mark and completion in 2028.

sources.title: World's Tallest Skyscraper Hits Major New Construction Milestone

claims.text: Bering Strait tunnel/bridge is a hypothetical 85-103km rail link between Chukotka (Russia) and Alaska (US) via the Diomede Islands, first dreamed by Tsar Nicholas II, revived periodically (2011 Russian plan, 2025 'Putin-Trump tunnel' floated by RDIF head Kirill Dmitriev to Elon Musk).

sources.title: A Japanese company is about to test a tiny space elevator in space

claims.text: Bering Strait crossing has no construction, no financing, and cost estimates ranging from ~$8bn (optimistic) to $65bn+ (traditional), requiring thousands of km of connecting rail through permafrost with no existing infrastructure.

sources.title: A Japanese company is about to test a tiny space elevator in space

claims.text: Atlantropa was German architect Hermann Sörgel's 1928 plan to dam the Strait of Gibraltar (14km at narrowest, dam planned 30km inside Med, 2.5km wide foundations, 300m high, crowned by 400m tower), plus dams at Sicily-Tunisia and Dardanelles, to lower the Mediterranean 100m (west) to 200m (east), draining one-fifth of the sea.

sources.title: Atlantropa: Herman Sörgel's Vision of a New Continent

claims.text: Atlantropa would have created 576,000 km2 of new land, generated 110,000 MW hydroelectricity (claimed 50% of Europe's needs at the time), and taken 100-150 years with 200,000 workers, uniting Europe and Africa into one continent; it was never built, rejected by Nazi regime and later made obsolete by nuclear power, decolonization and cost.

sources.title: Atlantropa: Herman Sörgel's Vision of a New Continent

claims.text: Sörgel promoted Atlantropa until his death in 1952 (struck by car on straight road, driver never found, murder speculation); Atlantropa Institute survived until 1960s.

sources.title: Atlantropa: Herman Sörgel's Vision of a New Continent

claims.text: Megaproject economics: Bent Flyvbjerg's database of >16,000 projects in 136 countries since 1910 finds 91.5% go over budget, over schedule, or both; <1% are on time, on budget and deliver promised benefits; mean cost overrun 62% with fat-tail risk.

sources.title: Why do large projects go over budget?

claims.text: Specific overruns: Channel Tunnel 80%, Denver International Airport 200%, Boston Big Dig 220%, Sydney Opera House 1,400%, James Webb Space Telescope 450%; 18% of IT projects overrun >50% with average 447% for that subset; nuclear plants and hydro dams have highest overruns and fattest tails.

sources.title: Why do large projects go over budget?

claims.text: Flyvbjerg defines megaprojects as >US$1bn; failure drivers include optimism bias, strategic misrepresentation, and sunk-cost lock-in ('start digging a hole so big there's no alternative').

sources.title: Why do large projects go over budget?

claims.text: Obayashi's own simulation concludes space elevator (96,000-km CNT cable, 400-m floating Earth Port, 12,500-ton counterweight, 100-ton climbers) is technically feasible only with assumed cable tensile strength of 150 GPa, taking roughly 20 years (20-ton seed cable reinforced 510 times to 7,000 tons over ~18 years + 1 year for facilities), with small wind/Coriolis effects and requirement to fix cable to Earth's surface with pre-tension; page states 'current technology levels are not yet sufficient to realize the concept, but our plan is realistic, and is a stepping stone.'

claims.text: Saudi authorities forcibly displaced Howeitat tribe members for NEOM/The Line: at least 47 arrested/detained per ALQST Feb 2023 'The Dark Side of Neom' (5 sentenced to death, 15 to 15-50 years, 19 detained with no information, 8 released); BBC reports >6,000 moved per government, ALQST estimates higher; satellite analysis shows villages al-Khuraybah, Sharma, Gayal demolished (homes/schools/hospitals wiped).

sources.title: Neom: Saudi forces 'told to kill' to clear land for eco-city
Neom: Saudi Arabia jails nearly 50 tribespeople for resisting displacement (ALQST 'The Dark Side of Neom')

claims.text: UN Human Rights Council independent experts (May 2023) said Howeitat evictions since Jan 2020 in three villages amount to forced evictions prohibited under international law (violation of right to adequate housing, freedom of expression, access to information), charged under 'overly vague' 2017 anti-terror law, with allegations of torture to extract confessions; three men sentenced to death 5 Aug 2022 (appeal 23 Jan 2023) and three to 27/35/50 years, not meeting 'most serious crimes' threshold for death penalty.

sources.title: Human rights experts alarmed over 'imminent executions' in Saudi Arabia

claims.text: BBC May 2024 investigation: ex-intelligence officer Col Rabih Alenezi testified he was ordered April 2020 to evict al-Khuraybah and that order stated Huwaitat were 'many rebels' and 'whoever continues to resist [eviction] should be killed' — licensing lethal force; Abdul Rahim al-Huwaiti was shot dead 13 April 2020 after refusing land valuation and posting protest videos (state claimed he opened fire; UN/NGOs say killed for resisting).

sources.title: Neom: Saudi forces 'told to kill' to clear land for eco-city

claims.text: EDF staff dissent: 73% of respondents in late-2022 FO union survey in hydro-engineering department opposed NEOM, saying it was contrary to EDF's ethical charter and net-zero 2050 commitment; staff argued Nestor pumped-hydro would be carbon-free but building NEOM would generate ~1.8 gigatonnes CO2 (4x UK annual emissions per UNSW estimate cited by Radio France); union sought right to withdraw for environmental/ethical reasons.

sources.title: Staff at France's EDF question involvement in futuristic Saudi city

claims.text: EDF contract terminated: Saudi authorities informed EDF March 2025 they no longer required Nestor hydro plant, opting for PV/wind/batteries for scaled-down NEOM; RFI notes The Line reduced to 2.4km as cost exploded from $500bn to $8.8tn estimate (Bloomberg); staff at La Motte-Servolex (30-40 employees, 3-4 years work) described abrupt stop as 'violent and depressing' while others called abandonment 'good news.'

sources.title: Saudi Arabia drops France's EDF from desert megacity project

claims.text: NEOM safety/engineering critique beyond wind/seismic: RFI citing WSJ/FT reports 100,000+ workers in area size of Belgium, overcrowded camps, inadequate infrastructure, absence of comprehensive emergency plan (2022 independent reports), and five fatal accidents in Nov 2024 at work sites/roads; new acting CEO Aiman al-Mudaifer launched comprehensive review in 'environment of limited resources' amid falling oil prices.

sources.title: Saudi Arabia drops France's EDF from desert megacity project

claims.text: Lantau/Kau Yi Chau environmental coalition opposition: 15 green groups released joint statement Nov 2021 urging Environmental Protection Department to reject rushed Lantau EIA (only two working days before press conference); Green Earth submission to LegCo warned reclamation would destroy Chinese white dolphin habitat (Grade 1 national protected animal) and require massive marine sand mining destroying river/sea beds; StoryMaps documents Lantau waters dolphin collapse from 188 in 2003 to 3-4 after airport reclamation, with 25% of Hong Kong coastline already reclaimed.

sources.title: Perseverance brought 3 Greenpeace projects to fruition – A look back at 2021
Can Hong Kong afford its planned artificial island construction project?
Hong Kong: Built on Borrowed Sea
Green group calls on Hong Kong government to cut back on Lantau reclamation project

claims.text: Lantau fiscal deficit critique: reclamation alone HK$580bn ($74bn) per government, veteran engineer Jason Poon estimates HK$900bn ($115bn) with infrastructure vs HK$400bn ($51bn) land-sale revenue = HK$500bn deficit; economist Andy Kwan warns fiscal reserves could be drained in a decade; Legislative Council lawmakers Jan 2025 urged delaying less-urgent projects to tackle ~HK$100bn deficit (double budget projection, similar to HK$101.6bn 2023-24); Real Estate Developers Association (Louis Loong) said government cannot support Lantau and Northern Metropolis concurrently and should permanently halt Lantau to avoid depressing Northern Metropolis land bids.

sources.title: Can Hong Kong afford its planned artificial island construction project?
Slow down on Hong Kong's less-urgent public projects to save money: lawmakers
Halt Lantau reclamation plan or risk Northern Metropolis bids: Hong Kong developers

claims.text: Lantau reclamation failure-risk base rate: Libre-research/Greenpeace Feb 2023 review of 52 artificial island projects worldwide found 46% incomplete/delayed/abandoned/vacant, rising to 77% for 13 mega-reclamations >1,000 ha (only one fully completed); former Hong Kong Observatory director Lam Chiu-ying argued project violates Xi Jinping's 'ecological civilization' principle and raises sea-level/flooding risks amid climate crisis.

claims.text: Atlantropa ecological/colonial critique: plan to lower Mediterranean 100m (west) to 200m (east) and expose 576,000 km2 would strand Venice/Genoa inland, increase Levant landmass 50%, disrupt salinity and climate (evaporative basin cut off from Atlantic), and was rejected as Eurocentric expansionism; Italians never supported it due to coastline dependence, Nazis ridiculed it as anti-Eurasian, and post-war nuclear power/decolonization rendered it technologically unnecessary and politically unfeasible.

sources.title: Atlantropa: Herman Sörgel's Vision of a New Continent

claims.text: Carbon-nanotube scalability skepticism quantified: best 2026 fluidics-aligned fiber achieves 12.5 GPa tensile strength (7.5 N/tex, 370 GPa modulus) approaching lower limit of individual CNTs (13-80 GPa), but still ~12x below Obayashi's required 150 GPa for 96,000km ribbon; paper notes macroscopic fibers to date exhibit only fraction of individual CNT properties due to alignment/packing defects, and only 15% strain stretching is possible without deterioration — supporting 'material does not exist at scale' is order-of-magnitude barrier.

sources.title: Improvement of the tensile strength of carbon nanotube fibers to 12.5 GPa by fluidics-induced alignment and densification

claims.text: Saudi fiscal oil-price sensitivity as structural blocker for NEOM: IMF/Oxford Economics breakeven $80-85/bbl vs Bloomberg $96 and all-in (incl. PIF domestic spending) >$110; Brent fell to $61-66 late 2025 (IMF baseline $66.94 for 2025, $62.38 for 2026) driving 2025 deficit ~SAR245bn (5.3% GDP) and Q1 2026 deficit SAR125.7bn ($33.5bn, largest since 2020) despite non-oil revenue SAR116.3bn; 2026 budget assumes deficit SAR165bn (3.3% GDP) at high-$60s/low-$70s oil, with public debt SAR1,457bn (31.7% GDP) end-2025 rising to SAR1,622bn (32.7%) end-2026.

sources.title: Saudi Fiscal Breakeven Oil Price 2026: $80-85 Estimate

claims.text: Oceanix regulatory/insurance vacuum and cost critique: no evidence of operational habitation beyond prototype design (6.3ha/12,000 residents) despite UN-Habitat May 2024 'being implemented' claim; profile's own gap notes no independent peer review of 3-4km spiral tube pressure design and no Korean legal framework for floating habitation/insurance; GlobalVoices base rate (46% incomplete, 77% for >1,000ha) implies floating-city scaling faces same fiscal/regulatory fat-tail as Lantau.

sources.title: Can Hong Kong afford its planned artificial island construction project?
